name: Fenfluramine

lead: Fenfluramine was a widely prescribed appetite suppressant, best known in the fen-phen combination, until it was withdrawn from the US market in 1997 after reports of heart valve disease.
A low-dose form is now sold as Fintepla for certain childhood epilepsies, not for weight loss.

paras: It releases serotonin and acts at 5-HT2 receptors, which reduces appetite; how it prevents seizures is not known.
The label carries a boxed warning for valvular heart disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension, and use requires echocardiogram monitoring through a restricted program.

lead: Fenfluramine is an amphetamine-derived serotonin-releasing drug. Introduced in France in 1963 and approved in the United States in 1973 as an appetite suppressant (brand name Pondimin), it was widely used for weight loss, often with phentermine in the combination known as fen-phen.[1][2]

It was withdrawn from the US market in 1997 after reports of heart valve disease and pulmonary hypertension in users.[1][3] Fenfluramine was reintroduced at lower doses as Fintepla, approved by the FDA in 2020 for seizures in Dravet syndrome and later Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, under a restricted program with echocardiogram monitoring.[1][4]

paras: Fenfluramine was prescribed for short-term obesity treatment. Wikipedia reports that about 5 million people in the US received fenfluramine or the related dexfenfluramine in 1996 to 1998, with or without phentermine.[1] The fen-phen combination was proposed in 1984 and was not FDA-approved as a combination.[1][3]
The current US label lists treatment of seizures associated with Dravet syndrome and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome in patients aged 2 and older.[4]

A 1997 report described valvular heart disease in patients who took fenfluramine with phentermine.[3] A study of appetite suppressants found an increased risk of primary pulmonary hypertension.[5] Laboratory work linked the valve findings to activation of 5-HT2B receptors.[6][7] The current label carries a boxed warning for valvular heart disease and pulmonary arterial hypertension, with echocardiograms required before, during and after treatment and distribution through a restricted program.[4] Other labeled effects include decreased appetite and weight, somnolence, suicidal behavior and ideation, serotonin syndrome and increased blood pressure.[4]

Fenfluramine releases serotonin, and its metabolite norfenfluramine acts at serotonin 5-HT2 receptors.[4][1] Animal work reported that it activates central melanocortin pathways, which may contribute to appetite suppression.[8] The label states that the mechanism of its seizure benefit is unknown.[4]

Phase 3 trials supported approval for Dravet syndrome and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, and further registered trials examine other epilepsies in infants and children, including CDKL5 deficiency disorder and Rett syndrome.[9][10] A trial on cognition has also been registered.[11] No recent trials of fenfluramine for appearance-related weight loss were found; the historical obesity evidence is described in the original approval-era studies and the harms reports above.

Fenfluramine was withdrawn in 1997 and later in other markets; India banned it in 1998.[1] It was removed from Schedule IV of the US Controlled Substances Act in December 2022.[1] In looksmaxxing and weight-loss discussions it appears mainly as a historical drug and cautionary example of appetite suppressants.
